lede: Tilt a floor far enough and a box that was sitting still starts to slide. Nothing new pushes it: the weight is the same as before, but part of it now points along the surface. Splitting the weight into those two parts is the whole of this topic.
can: Resolve a weight into its components along and perpendicular to a slope
Decide which component takes the sine, from the shape of the problem rather than a mnemonic
Write the equation of motion for a body going up a slope and for the same body coming down

text: Turn the axes onto the slope

alt: A block on a slope at angle alpha. Friction F acts up the slope, along the plane; the normal reaction R acts at right angles to the plane; the weight mg acts straight down, along neither.

caption: The friction and the reaction already lie along the two new axes; only the weight does not.

md: Instead of horizontal and vertical, use **along the plane** and **perpendicular to it**. Friction and any applied force already lie along the plane, and the normal reaction lies across it, so each goes into its equation whole. Only a force pointing along neither axis has to be split.

stem: A 1.5 kg block is held still on a rough slope by friction. Sort its three forces onto the two axes.

steps.decision: It acts along the surface of the slope, so it already lies on the first axis.

steps.working: Normal reaction $R$: perpendicular to the plane
steps.decision: The surface pushes out at right angles to itself: the second axis.
Vertical lies along neither axis, so this force is split into a part along the plane and a part across it.

prompt: On an inclined plane, which force is the one that has to be resolved into components?
explain: As step 3 of See it found, the weight points straight down, along neither axis, so it is the one force to resolve. Friction already lies along the plane and the normal reaction across it, so both go in whole.

twin.prompt: A rope parallel to the plane pulls a crate up a slope. Which force goes into the along-slope equation without being resolved?
twin.explain: The rope lies along the plane, so its pull goes in as it stands. The weight has to be resolved first, and the normal reaction has no part along the slope at all.

optionNotes.why: The weight points straight down, along neither axis, so only its part along the slope goes into that equation.
The reaction is at right angles to the slope, so it belongs in the perpendicular equation and has no part along the slope.
It already lies at right angles to the plane, on the second axis, so it goes into the perpendicular equation whole.
It acts along the surface of the slope, on the first axis, so it goes into the along-slope equation as it stands.

text: Where the sine and cosine come from

The angle alpha is marked at the foot of the slope and again between the weight and the component into the slope.

caption: The weight and its two parts: the angle α appears again between the weight and the part into the slope.

md: The plane is at $\alpha$ to the horizontal, so the line perpendicular to it is at $\alpha$ to the vertical: turning both lines through $90°$ keeps the angle between them. The weight is vertical, so it makes the angle $\alpha$ with the perpendicular. In the right-angled triangle it builds, the side next to $\alpha$ is $mg\cos\alpha$, into the slope, and the side opposite is $mg\sin\alpha$, along it.

stem: A 7 kg box rests on a 25° slope. Find the two parts of the box's weight: along the slope and into it.

steps.decision: The force to split, in newtons.
Opposite the angle in the weight's triangle, so the sine.
Next to the angle, so the cosine.

prompt: A body of weight 90 N sits on a 40° slope. What is the weight's part along the slope, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: Along the slope is the side opposite $\alpha$, so it takes the sine, as step 2 of See it did: $90\sin 40° = 57.85$ N. The cosine gives 68.94 N, the part pressing into the slope.

twin.prompt: A crate of weight 130 N sits on a 35° slope. What is the part of its weight pressing into the slope, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: Into the slope is the side next to the angle, so the cosine: $130\cos 35° = 106.49$ N.

text: Why the flat-slope check never fails

md: Rebuild the rule rather than memorise it. Imagine the slope almost flat. The body would barely slide, so the part along the slope is nearly zero, and $\sin 0° = 0$. The ground would take nearly the whole weight, so the part into the slope is nearly $mg$, and $\cos 0° = 1$.

title: Why the check is worth more than the rule
md: A remembered rule is the first thing to go under pressure, and this is the most repeated slip on the topic: Summer 2019 Q6 and Summer 2025 Q6 both report sine and cosine swapped. The flat-slope test rebuilds both parts from something you cannot forget: a flat floor holds a body up and lets it slide nowhere.

stem: A student writes the part of a 50 N weight along a 15° slope as $50\cos 15°$. Check it before using it.

steps.decision: An extreme case settles the choice before any arithmetic.
A flat floor cannot drag a body along it with its whole weight, so the cosine fails.
Nothing drives a body along a flat floor, so the sine passes.
The checked function, used at the real angle.

prompt: A slope is made steeper and steeper, until it is almost vertical. Which part of the weight becomes nearly the whole weight?
explain: Run the See it check at the other extreme: as $\alpha$ nears $90°$, $\sin\alpha$ nears 1 and $\cos\alpha$ nears 0. So the part along the slope becomes nearly the whole weight: the body is almost falling freely, and the surface barely touches it.

twin.prompt: A slope is made flatter, from 60° to 30°. What happens to the part of the weight pressing into the slope?
twin.explain: Flatter moves towards the flat floor, where the surface takes the whole weight. The part into the slope is $mg\cos\alpha$, and $\cos 30° = 0.87$ is larger than $\cos 60° = 0.5$.

optionNotes.why: Flatter moves towards the flat floor, where the surface takes the whole weight, so the part pressing into the slope grows.
The part into the slope is $mg\cos\alpha$, which changes with the angle, so tilting the slope changes it.
That part shrinks as the slope steepens, because $\cos\alpha$ falls towards 0; it is the flat-floor case where it is nearly the whole weight.
The two parts always rebuild the whole weight, so as one shrinks the other grows towards the full weight.

text: Across the slope, the forces balance

md: A body accelerating on a slope is not in equilibrium, but it is not far off. Perpendicular to the plane the forces always balance, because nothing sinks into the surface or lifts off it, so $R = mg\cos\alpha$. Along the plane there is a resultant, and that is where the acceleration comes from.

stem: A 2 kg block slides down a 40° slope against 5 N of friction. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration.

steps.decision: The weight's part pressing into the surface.
Nothing moves across the slope, so the reaction balances that part exactly.
Down the slope positive, friction against the slide: a force is left over.
The left-over force is what accelerates the block.

prompt: A sledge speeds up as it slides down a rough slope. What is true of the forces on it?
options: The perpendicular forces balance but the along-slope forces do not
The along-slope forces balance but the perpendicular ones do not
answer: The perpendicular forces balance but the along-slope forces do not
explain: Across the slope nothing sinks in or lifts off, so the forces balance, as $R = 15.32$ N did in See it. Along the slope a force is left over, which is why the body speeds up; if everything balanced it would not accelerate.

twin.prompt: A block moves down a rough slope at a steady speed. What is true of the forces on it?
options: The forces balance along and across the slope
twin.answer: The forces balance along and across the slope
twin.explain: Constant speed means no acceleration, so there is no resultant along the slope either: the weight's part along it equals the friction. Across the slope the forces balance as always.

optionNotes.why: That is true of a body speeding up; at a constant speed there is no acceleration, so the along-slope forces balance too.
Nothing ever sinks into the slope or lifts off it, so the perpendicular forces always balance as well.
If every force balanced there would be no resultant, but the body is speeding up, so something is left over along the slope.

optionNotes.option: The along-slope forces balance but the perpendicular ones do not
optionNotes.why: It is the other way round: nothing moves into or out of the surface, while along it the body speeds up.

text: The two things CCEA fixes for you

caption: The pull P is parallel to the plane, and the friction F is a number you are given.

md: Two restrictions make this topic smaller than it looks on other boards. An applied force **always acts parallel to the plane**, so it never needs resolving. Friction is **given**, as a value or as so many newtons per kilogram: $F = \mu R$ is not on this specification. The normal reaction still belongs on every diagram.

stem: A 13 kg box is pulled up a 15° slope by 60 N parallel to it, against 8 N of friction. Find the resultant up the slope.

steps.working: Pull: 60 N along the plane, in as it stands
steps.decision: It already lies along the slope, so it needs no resolving.
Given as a value, and the box moves up, so it acts down.

steps.working: Weight's part down the slope: $130\sin 15° = 33.65$ N
steps.decision: The weight is the only force resolved.
Up positive: the pull minus both forces against it.

prompt: A CCEA slope question adds a push or a pull on the body. How is it directed?
options: At whatever angle the question chooses
explain: The Teacher Guidance fixes it: any push or pull on a CCEA slope acts parallel to the plane, like the 60 N pull in See it. That is why the weight is the only force you ever resolve here.

twin.prompt: On a CCEA slope question, how is the friction on the body given?
options: As a value, or per kilogram of mass
As μR, from the normal reaction
Never: you work it out from the angle
twin.answer: As a value, or per kilogram of mass
twin.explain: CCEA gives the friction, as a number of newtons or as so many newtons per kilogram. $F = \mu R$ is not on this specification, and the angle fixes only the weight's parts.

optionNotes.option: As μR, from the normal reaction
optionNotes.why: $F = \mu R$ is A-level mechanics and is not on this specification; CCEA gives the friction to you.

optionNotes.option: Never: you work it out from the angle
optionNotes.why: The angle fixes the weight's two parts, not the friction, which the question gives as a value or per kilogram.
A horizontal push would need resolving on a slope, and CCEA rules that out: every applied force on its slopes acts along the plane.

optionNotes.option: At whatever angle the question chooses
optionNotes.why: Other boards set pulls at an angle to the plane, but CCEA's Teacher Guidance keeps every applied force parallel to it.

md: Sliding down, the weight's part along the slope drives the body and friction opposes it. Take down the slope as positive, so the acceleration comes out positive, and find $R$ first if it is asked.

stem: A 12 kg box slides down a 25° slope against 20 N of friction. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration.

steps.decision: Perpendicular balance gives the reaction.
The part of the weight that drives the slide.
Friction opposes the motion, so it comes off.
Positive, so the box speeds up down the slope.

prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². A 17 kg crate slides down a 30° slope against 34 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: Sliding down, the weight's part drives and friction opposes, as in step 3 of See it: $170\sin 30° = 85$ N, so $85 - 34 = 17a$ and $a = 3$ m/s².

twin.prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². A 16 kg sack slides down a 20° slope against 20 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s², to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: $160\sin 20° = 54.72$ N drives it and the friction opposes: $54.72 - 20 = 16a$, so $a = 2.17$ m/s².

md: The push is parallel to the plane, so only the weight needs resolving. The block moves up, so friction and the weight's part along the slope both act down it, against the push.

stem: A 8 kg block is pushed up a 25° slope by 70 N parallel to it, against 12 N of friction. Find its acceleration.

steps.working: Weight's part down the slope: $80\sin 25° = 33.81$ N
steps.decision: Resolve the weight only.
Both forces against the push are subtracted.
Positive, so it speeds up the slope.

prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². A 9 kg block is pulled up a 15° slope by 80 N parallel to it, against 11 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s², to 2 decimal places?
explain: Going up, the weight's part and the friction both act against the pull, as in step 2 of See it. The weight is $90$ N, its part down the slope $90\sin 15° = 23.29$ N, so $80 - 23.29 - 11 = 9a$ and $a = 5.08$ m/s².

twin.prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². An 11 kg trunk is pulled up an 18° slope by 90 N parallel to it, against 10 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s², to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: $110\sin 18° = 33.99$ N and the friction both oppose the pull: $90 - 33.99 - 10 = 11a$, so $a = 4.18$ m/s².

caption: Change the direction of travel and exactly one arrow moves: the friction.

md: Friction opposes the motion, so it points up the slope when the body slides down and down the slope when the body moves up. Nothing else on the diagram changes. Going up, the weight's part and friction add, so a body always slows harder going up than it speeds up coming down.
Summer 2019 Q6 compared exactly this: work each acceleration in its own direction of travel, so both come out positive, and only then compare sizes.

stem: A 6 kg block is on a 35° slope, with 10 N of friction whichever way it moves. Find its acceleration sliding down and its deceleration moving up.

steps.working: Weight's part: $60\sin 35° = 34.41$ N down the slope
steps.decision: The same in both directions of travel: work it out once.
Friction points up the slope, against the slide.

steps.working: Moving up: $34.41 + 10 = 6a$, so the deceleration is $7.40$ m/s²
steps.decision: Friction turns round and joins the weight's part.

title: FM Mechanics Incline Plane
why: Taught against this specification by name, so its restrictions are built in. Watch the axes go onto the slope before any force is resolved.

prompt: One block, one rough slope: it is released to slide down, then projected up it. Which is larger in size?
explain: Only friction turns round. Going up, it joins the weight's part, as in step 3 of See it: 7.40 m/s² against 4.07 m/s² coming down. So the deceleration going up is the larger.

twin.prompt: A block projected up a rough slope slows at 7 m/s². Sliding back down, how does its acceleration compare?
twin.explain: Going up, the friction and the weight's part add. Coming down, the friction works against the weight's part, so less is left over and the acceleration is smaller.

optionNotes.why: Going up, friction and the weight's part add; coming down, friction opposes the weight's part, so less is left over.
That needs the same resultant both ways, but friction turns round, so the two resultants differ.
Coming down, friction works against the weight's part, so less is left over than going up, where the two add.
Only the friction turns round, and that changes the resultant: going up the two forces add, coming down they partly cancel.

prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². A 19 kg body is projected up a 30° slope against 38 N of friction. What is its deceleration, in m/s²?
explain: Going up, friction joins the weight's part, as in step 3 of See it: $190\sin 30° = 95$ N, so $95 + 38 = 19a$ and the deceleration is 7 m/s².

twin.prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². A 6 kg body is projected up a 25° slope against 9 N of friction. What is its deceleration, in m/s², to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: Both act down the slope: $60\sin 25° + 9 = 34.36$ N, so the deceleration is $34.36 \div 6 = 5.73$ m/s².

md: A block sent up a slope has no push. The weight's part along the slope and the friction both act down it, so the block decelerates. A constant-acceleration formula then says how far it goes; a stopping distance given first hands you the deceleration instead (2021).

stem: A 6 kg block is sent up a 22° slope at 9 m/s against 15 N of friction. How far does it travel before it stops?

steps.decision: Both forces point down the slope.
Divide by the mass.
It stops, so $v = 0$; it is slowing, so the $2as$ term is taken off.
Solve for the distance.

prompt: A block moving up a slope at 6 m/s decelerates at 4 m/s². How far up the slope does it travel before it stops, in metres?
explain: It stops, so $v = 0$, and a deceleration of 4 means $a = -4$, as the stopping line of See it did: $0 = 6^2 - 2 \times 4 \times s$, so $s = 36 \div 8 = 4.5$ m.

md: **Mark the forces** (2021, 2024, 2025). Three arrows: the weight straight down, the reaction at right angles to the slope, and friction against the motion. $mg\sin\alpha$ is part of the weight, not a fourth force; the 2024 report saw that extra arrow down the slope often.

stem: An 11 kg box slides down a rough 25° slope. Mark its forces, then find the pull along the slope.

steps.decision: Drawn once, from the centre of the box.

steps.working: Reaction $R$: at right angles to the slope
steps.decision: The surface pushes out, never along.
It opposes the slide.
Found from the weight arrow, never drawn as another force.

prompt: A crate slides down a rough slope. A student marks four forces on it: the weight straight down, the normal reaction, friction up the slope, and a force pulling it down the slope. Which arrow should not be there?
explain: The See it drew three forces and no more. The pull down the slope is the weight's own component, and the weight is already drawn, so drawing it again counts it twice. The 2024 report saw that extra arrow often, and an extra force costs the diagram mark.

twin.prompt: A force parallel to a rough slope pushes a crate up it. How many forces go on its diagram?
twin.explain: The weight, the normal reaction, friction down the slope and the push itself. The weight's part along the slope is not a fifth force; it is already inside the weight arrow.

optionNotes.why: The push is a fourth force, beside the weight, the normal reaction and the friction down the slope.
The weight's part along the slope is not a separate force; drawing it as well counts the weight twice.
The surface pushes on the crate at right angles to the slope, so the reaction is a real force and belongs on the diagram.
The slope is rough and the crate slides down, so friction acts up the slope and must be drawn.

text: Exam twist: a value to show

md: **A value to show** (2021, 2024). A deceleration or a friction force is printed for you to show. The equation goes in with the letter still in it; the value must come out, not go in. The 2024 report saw many put the printed value into an equation instead.

stem: A 8 kg box moves up a 20° slope against 12 N of friction. Show that its deceleration is 5 m/s², to the nearest whole number.

steps.decision: The equation with $a$ still in it: both forces act down the slope.
Collect the numbers on one side.

steps.working: $a = -4.92$: a deceleration of 4.92, which is 5 to the nearest whole number
steps.decision: The printed value comes out last.

prompt: A part says: show that the deceleration of the box up the slope is 4 m/s², to the nearest whole number. What should your working do?
options: Form the equation of motion and solve it for a
Put a = 4 into the equation and check that it balances
Quote v = u + at with a = 4
answer: Form the equation of motion and solve it for a
explain: A show-that is marked on the method: the equation formed with $a$ still in it, then solved, so the printed value comes out last, as on the last line of See it. The 2024 report saw many put the given value into an equation instead; only the full method earned full marks.

twin.prompt: A part says: show that the friction on the sledge is 18 N. Which working earns full marks?
options: Resolve, form the equation with F in it, and solve for F
Put F = 18 into the equation and check both sides agree
State F = 18 N on the force diagram
twin.answer: Resolve, form the equation with F in it, and solve for F
twin.explain: The marks are for the derivation: the equation with the letter in it, then its solution. Checking the printed value is verification, capped below full marks.

optionNotes.option: Put F = 18 into the equation and check both sides agree
optionNotes.why: That verifies the printed value instead of deriving it, which CCEA caps below full marks.

optionNotes.option: State F = 18 N on the force diagram
optionNotes.why: The printed value earns nothing on its own: the marks are for the equation and its solution.

optionNotes.option: Put a = 4 into the equation and check that it balances
optionNotes.why: That checks the printed value rather than deriving it, which CCEA caps below full marks.

optionNotes.option: Quote v = u + at with a = 4
optionNotes.why: It starts from the printed value, so it shows nothing: the deceleration has to come out of the forces.

md: **Friction per kilogram** (2025). The friction is given in newtons per kilogram of mass. First line: multiply by the body's own mass before it goes into the equation. It is a one-line conversion, and it carries its own mark.

stem: A 18 kg box slides down a 25° slope, and the friction is 3 N per kg of mass. Find its acceleration.

steps.decision: Per kilogram, so multiply by the body's own mass.
Down positive; the friction opposes the slide.
Divide by the mass.

prompt: A 7 kg box is sliding down a rough slope, with friction of 3 N per kg of mass. What goes into the equation of motion for the friction?
explain: Per kilogram means each of the box's 7 kg is resisted by 3 N, so multiply by its own mass, as step 1 of See it did: $3 \times 7 = 21$ N.

twin.prompt: A 12 kg sledge meets friction of 1.5 N per kg of mass. What friction force goes into its equation?
twin.explain: $1.5 \times 12 = 18$ N: every one of its 12 kilograms is resisted by 1.5 N.

optionNotes.why: That is the friction on one kilogram only; multiply by the sledge's 12 kg.
120 N is the sledge's weight; per kilogram means multiply by the mass, 12, not by the weight.
That is the friction on one kilogram only; the box has 7 of them, so multiply by 7.
70 N is the box's weight, $7 \times 10$; the friction per kilogram multiplies the mass, not $g$.

md: The hardest shape so far (2021) runs the whole trip: up, stop, and back to the start. Here a 5 kg block leaves $A$ at 6 m/s up a 20° slope and stops at $B$, 3.6 m further up.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Friction as $F = \mu R$, a force at an angle to the plane, and two connected bodies on a slope are A-level mechanics. CCEA's slopes carry one body, with any push parallel to the plane and the friction given.

stem: A 5 kg block leaves $A$ at 6 m/s up a 20° slope, stops at $B$ after 3.6 m, then slides back. Find its speed back at $A$.

steps.decision: The stopping distance gives the deceleration before any force.
Going up, the weight's part and friction both slow it.
A new equation: friction has turned round to act up the slope.
From rest at $B$, over the same distance.

prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². After stopping, a 22 kg block slides back down a 30° slope against 33 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: On the way back down, friction turns round to act up the slope, as in step 3 of See it, while the weight's part still acts down it: $220\sin 30° = 110$ N, so $110 - 33 = 22a$ and $a = 3.5$ m/s².

twin.prompt: Take $g = 10$ m/s². A 24 kg block that has stopped on a 30° slope slides back down against 48 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
twin.explain: Friction now acts up the slope: $240\sin 30° - 48 = 24a$, so $72 = 24a$ and $a = 3$ m/s².

md:
Rotate the axes onto the slope and resolve the weight: $mg\sin\alpha$ along, $mg\cos\alpha$ across.
Rebuild which part takes the sine from the flat-slope test.
Find $R$ from perpendicular balance, and the acceleration along the plane.
Write the equation for each direction of travel, with friction turned round.
Spot the twists: the diagram, a value to show, friction per kilogram, the return trip.

Most years this is a whole question: mark the forces, find the normal reaction or show a value, write the equation of motion, then the return trip or a speed or a distance. The equation earns one mark for the resultant along the slope, resolved with the sine, and one for $= ma$; the last is the value, positive in the direction of travel. Stuck? Axes on the slope first, then the direction of motion.
